blocks.prompt: The Whale With the Unicorn Tooth
blocks.text: The narwhal is a whale. It lives in the cold Arctic sea, and it swims under big sheets of ice. A male narwhal has one long tusk on the front of his head. The tusk is not a horn. The tusk is a tooth. It grows right through his lip and out into the water. It can grow longer than a car. Long ago, people found narwhal tusks and sold them. They said the tusks came from unicorns. They cost a lot of money. But there was never a unicorn. There was only a whale, swimming quietly under the ice.

blocks.prompt: The Tooth That Looks Like a Spear
blocks.text: Narwhals are whales, and they live farther north than almost any other whale. Their home is the Arctic, where the sea freezes over for months at a time. Narwhals have no fin on their back. A tall fin would scrape the ice above them, so they swim with a smooth, low ridge instead. When the ice closes in, they find a crack, push their heads up, and take a breath. The strangest thing about a narwhal is its tusk. Most male narwhals grow one, and it can reach ten feet, longer than a bed. It is not a horn. It is a tooth. It is the whale's left front tooth, and it never stops growing. It pushes out through the whale's lip and into the sea. It always twists the same way, spiraling to the left like a candy cane. Nobody was sure what the tusk was for. Then scientists looked closely and found something surprising. The tusk is full of tiny nerves, millions of them, running from the cold water outside all the way to the whale's brain. The tusk can feel. Cameras have also caught narwhals tapping fish with their tusks, stunning them before eating.

blocks.prompt: The Unicorn Horn That Came From a Whale
blocks.text: For hundreds of years, Europe believed in unicorns, and it had the horns to prove it. Kings kept them locked in treasure rooms. Doctors ground them into powder and sold the dust as medicine, promising it could cure sickness and find poison hidden in a cup of wine. A single horn could cost more than a house. In 1577, the explorer Martin Frobisher carried one home from the Arctic and presented it to Queen Elizabeth the First, who kept it with the crown jewels. Every one of those horns came from a whale. The narwhal is an Arctic whale and a close cousin of the beluga. It spends its life among the drifting sea ice north of Canada, Greenland, and Russia, in water no unicorn has ever walked on. Male narwhals grow a single tusk that can pass ten feet in length. It is not a horn at all. It is a tooth. The whale's left front tooth simply refuses to stop growing, boring straight out through the upper lip and into the freezing water. It spirals as it goes, and it always spirals the same direction, counterclockwise, whether the whale swims off Greenland or off Russia. Norse hunters knew exactly where the tusks came from. They also knew that a buyer in Europe would pay a fortune for a unicorn horn and almost nothing for a whale tooth, so for roughly four hundred years they kept quiet and kept selling. The secret finally broke in the 1600s, when a Danish scholar named Ole Worm showed his audience the skull the tusk was still attached to. The unicorn trade collapsed. The whale had been there the whole time, swimming under the ice, waiting to be believed in.

blocks.prompt: The Whale That Feels With Its Tooth
blocks.text: The narwhal spends its whole life in water that would kill you in minutes. It lives at the top of the world, in the cracks and open leads between plates of Arctic sea ice, north of Canada and Greenland. Everything about its body is shaped by that ice. It has no fin on its back, because a tall fin would catch on the ceiling. It is mottled gray as a calf and fades paler as it ages, until the oldest males look like weathered ivory. It can dive more than 4,500 feet straight down, hold its breath for twenty-five minutes, and surface through a breathing hole no wider than a bathtub. And it has a tooth like a spear. The tusk grows from the left side of the upper jaw, punches through the lip, and spirals out into the sea, counterclockwise, always counterclockwise, sometimes past ten feet. Almost every tusk belongs to a male. For centuries the obvious guess was that the tusk is a weapon, and the obvious guess appears to be wrong. Nobody has ever documented narwhals fighting seriously with them. What people have documented is stranger. Cut across a narwhal tusk and the arrangement is backward. Our teeth are hard on the outside and softer within. The narwhal's is porous and soft on the outside and hard at its core, which means seawater seeps inward toward something like ten million nerve endings wired straight to the brain. The tusk is not armor. It is an instrument. Researchers think the whale may be reading the water through its tooth, sensing shifts in saltiness that hint at ice forming ahead, or at where the fish have gone. Then, in 2017, a drone hovering over Tremblay Sound caught narwhals doing something nobody had proposed. They were tapping Arctic cod with the tips of their tusks, stunning the fish, and swallowing them. One piece of footage added a use that four hundred years of guessing had missed. Which raises a useful question. If we have been wrong, or half right, about this animal's most obvious feature for four centuries, what else are we sure about that we have simply never watched closely enough?

6.title: The Whale With the Unicorn Tooth
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Whale With the Unicorn Tooth

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Monodon monoceros: one tooth, one horn
Tusk structure is inverted: hard core, porous surface
Roughly 10 million nerve endings inside
About 15 percent of females grow a small tusk
Tusking: males cross tusks gently at the surface
Responds to danger by freezing, not fleeing

blocks.prompt: The Tooth Nobody Can Explain
blocks.text: Ask a biologist what the narwhal's tusk is for and you will get a careful answer, which is a polite way of saying that nobody is certain. This should be surprising. We have sequenced the animal's genome and tracked it by satellite across the Arctic, and yet its single most obvious feature remains an open question. That gap is worth sitting with, because it shows how science actually behaves when the evidence refuses to settle. Start with what is not in doubt. The tusk is a tooth. It is the narwhal's left front tooth, and rather than staying politely inside the mouth it grows forward through the upper lip and simply keeps going, sometimes past ten feet. It spirals counterclockwise, without exception, on every narwhal ever measured. Its structure is inside out compared with our own teeth: hard at the core, soft and porous at the surface, so that seawater can seep inward toward roughly ten million nerve endings. Usually only males grow one. Roughly one female in seven grows a smaller version. Very occasionally a whale grows two. Now the arguments. The oldest explanation is the simplest: the tusk is a weapon, and males fight with it. The trouble is that no one has ever filmed a serious narwhal duel, and a slender ten foot tooth makes a poor lance. A second explanation calls the tusk a sensory organ, and the porous surface and the nerve count support it. The dentist and researcher Martin Nweeia has argued that the whale may effectively taste the sea through its tooth, reading salt and temperature as it swims. A third explanation treats the tusk as an advertisement, like a peacock's tail: expensive to grow, useless in a fight, and therefore honest proof that the male carrying it is strong enough to waste energy on it. Males do cross tusks gently at the surface, a behavior called tusking, which fits display better than combat. Then, in 2017, a drone caught narwhals doing something no theory had predicted: tapping Arctic cod with the tips of their tusks, stunning the fish before swallowing them. None of these ideas cancels the others. A tooth can sense the water, impress a rival, and swat a fish. The honest position is that the tusk is probably doing several jobs at once, and that we noticed the fourth job only because somebody finally put a camera in the right patch of sky. Meanwhile the question is getting harder to answer, not easier. Narwhals are built for ice, and the Arctic is losing it. As the ice retreats, killer whales push north into water that used to be closed to them, and the narwhal's answer to danger is to go still and silent rather than flee, a strategy designed for hiding under ice, not for outrunning orcas. Ships follow the open water too, and narwhals are among the most noise sensitive whales ever measured. We may end up answering the oldest question about this animal at the exact moment we stop being able to ask it in the wild.
